headline: New moon springs load up the Stratford Shoal rip as fluke slide into the channels
subhead: Bigger tides and a sunset flood window are setting up the best striper stretch since the June full moon — if the wind cooperates.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does in early July — it built heat on top and shuffled bait around underneath. Surface temps in the back bays and harbors climbed into the mid-to-upper 70s, and that warm cap pushed a lot of the bait — and the fluke that were eating it — out of the shallow flats and into the channels and inlets where there's still cooler water moving. I saw it in Oyster Bay and again poking around the mouth of the Norwalk Islands: bait balled up tight against structure instead of spread out over the flats like it was in June. Wind was mostly out of the south and southwest for stretches, which didn't help clarity, but it never blew hard enough to really wreck things — just enough to keep the surface stirred and the fishing a notch tougher than it should've been.

This week the moon is the story. We're running up on new moon and the spring tides that come with it, with the peak alignment landing July 11-13. That means bigger tidal swings than we've had since the full moon in June, and — this is the part I care about — the PM flood is going to converge with sunset through that stretch. That's the first evening window like this since last month, and in the Central Sound that combination (big water moving, low light, bait getting squeezed through the narrows) is when the bigger bass show themselves. I'd circle Friday through Monday evening on the calendar. If the wind lays down out of the south for those sunsets, the flood pushing through the Stratford Shoal rip and around the Norwalk Islands should set up about as good as it gets for July.

On the striper front, it's been a real fish but not an easy one. Guys working bunker schools around Middle Ground Light and along the Connecticut shoreline near Charles Island have had good mornings snagging and drifting live bunker on wire leaders, picking off fish in the 20s of pounds mixed with a lot of schoolies. The bite windows are short — usually the last hour of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, right when the current starts moving bait off the structure. At Stratford Shoal itself, the rip has been holding fish on the drop, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when the water piles up and pushes bait off the shoal edge into the deeper channel — I've had the best luck there drifting eels or bucktailing 1.5 to 2-ounce white and chartreuse jigs along the break in 20 to 35 feet. Nothing has been stacked up thick, but the fish that are there have some size to them, which tracks with what other boats have been finding scattered from here out to Block Island and the Cape this summer — pockets of bigger bass, not blitzes.

Bluefish have filled in the gaps nicely and are the more reliable bite right now. Wherever the bunker schools have been getting worked over — off Eaton's Neck, around the Norwalk Islands, and in close to the Connecticut beaches near New Haven — the blues have been all over them on top, especially in the first hour of light. Bucktails, poppers, or just cut bunker chunks fished under a float will get bit. It's not subtle fishing and it's a good one to bring kids or a buddy who wants steady action without needing a tide chart memorized.

Fluke is where I'd spend my daylight hours this week, because the pattern is clear: the fish have followed the cooler water out of the warmed-up bays and into the channels, cuts, and inlet mouths. The mouth of the Norwalk Islands channel, the deeper cuts around Charles Island, and the Port Jeff Harbor entrance have all been holding fish on the outgoing tide, when the current sweeps bait — and Gulp — off the flats and funnels it through the deeper water. Five-inch white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom in 20 to 40 feet, have been the most consistent producer. It's not a doormat parade — most days you're culling through shorts for a couple of keepers in the 3 to 5-pound range — but it beats fishing the flats right now, where the warm water has the fish either buried deep or just not interested.

Porgies have been the steady, dependable bite all week, and I mean that as a compliment in a summer where a lot of species have been streaky. The reefs around the Norwalk Islands and the rockpiles off Charles Island are loaded, and simple bottom rigs with sandworms or clam pieces in 15 to 30 feet will keep a rod bent most of an afternoon. Good one to fall back on if the tide's wrong for stripers or the fluke aren't cooperating.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, have been a no-show in my part of the Sound, and the broader data backs that up — warm water alone hasn't been enough to trigger a real push this year. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

Looking ahead, the window I'm most interested in is that Friday-through-Monday flood/sunset stretch on the new moon springs. If the wind holds out of the south and stays light in the evenings, I'd be at the Stratford Shoal rip or working the Norwalk Islands current lines right as the sun drops and the flood really gets moving — that's historically when the bigger bass commit. Plan B if the bass don't show is simple: work the fluke through the channel cuts on the strong outgoing that comes with these bigger tides, because more water moving means more bait getting flushed, and that's exactly the kind of current fluke like to sit in and ambush.
